items.question: Your template HTML-encodes every user value, so `<` becomes `<`. A value still ends up inside `<a href="{{url}}">` and an attacker submits `javascript:alert(1)`. Why did encoding not help?
items.answer: HTML entity encoding protects markup structure, but in the href the value is interpreted as a URL, and `javascript:` is valid URL syntax, so the browser executes it on click. The value needs URL-context handling: validate or allowlist the scheme (http, https, or relative paths) and encode for the URL context, not just entity-encode for HTML.
items.trap: The naive answer is 'we escape everything, so we are safe'. Escaping is context-dependent: HTML-body encoding does nothing to stop a dangerous URL scheme inside an attribute the browser treats as a URL. The rule is to encode for the specific output context (HTML, attribute, URL, or JavaScript).

items.question: All user input passes through a server-side HTML sanitizer before storage. Is the app now immune to XSS?
items.answer: No. Stored and reflected XSS through server output are covered, but DOM-based XSS happens in the browser: client-side script reads a source like location.hash or postMessage and writes it into a sink such as innerHTML. That data never crossed your server sanitizer. You must review client-side DOM sinks separately and keep framework escaping on for rendered output.
items.trap: The common answer assumes XSS is one server-side filtering problem. Server-side filtering alone does not cover DOM-based XSS, and the primary defense is context-aware output encoding at the point of use, with sanitization reserved for cases where users must author HTML.

items.question: We set SameSite=Lax on the session cookie. Is that enough to retire our CSRF tokens?
items.answer: No. Lax still sends the cookie on top-level cross-site GET navigations, so any state change reachable via GET stays exposed. SameSite and Origin or Fetch Metadata checks are defense in depth: every state-changing endpoint still needs a server-validated CSRF token, and state-changing operations must stay out of GET.
items.trap: The naive reasoning is 'SameSite blocks cross-site requests, so CSRF is impossible'. Lax is a partial browser-side mitigation, not a server-validated guarantee, and it does nothing for GET-based state changes or clients whose cookie behavior differs.

items.question: Every mutating endpoint validates a synchronizer token. A pentest still reports that one stored XSS gives them full account takeover. How, if CSRF was 'solved'?
items.answer: Because XSS is a strictly stronger attack. Script running on your origin operates inside the victim's session: it can read the token from the page or from any cookie the page can access, then issue same-origin requests that carry both the session cookie and a valid token. CSRF defenses assume the attacker cannot run script on your origin, so preventing XSS is a prerequisite, not an alternative.
items.trap: The common answer treats CSRF and XSS as independent boxes. CSRF tokens defend against a malicious third-party site, not against script already executing on your own pages; XSS can defeat CSRF controls.

items.question: The API returns no CORS headers at all. Did the browser stop the evil site's request from reaching the server?
items.answer: Not necessarily. For requests that do not trigger a preflight (form posts, images, simple fetch calls) the request is still sent and the server still processes it; the same-origin policy and CORS stop the evil page's JavaScript from reading the response. That is why state-changing endpoints need CSRF defenses and server-side authorization regardless of CORS.
items.trap: The widespread misconception is that SOP or CORS blocks the request itself. CORS is a read policy enforced around the response; the request often fires and its side effects execute before any CORS check matters.

items.question: We never configured CORS, so our API is private and only our frontend can use it, right?
items.answer: No. CORS only controls which origins a browser will let script read responses from. It is not an authentication mechanism and does not make an endpoint private: curl, a server-side client, or any non-browser tool ignores it entirely. The server must authenticate and authorize every request independently of CORS.
items.trap: The naive answer conflates 'my browser app cannot read it cross-origin' with 'nobody can call it'. CORS is a browser read-access mechanism; privacy and authorization come from authentication and server-side policy.

items.question: Why is a nonce-based `script-src` considered stricter than allowlisting script hosts like `https://cdn.example.com`?
items.answer: A nonce policy is tied to the exact scripts intentionally emitted in that specific response: any other inline or injected script without the nonce is blocked. A host allowlist trusts every script that host will ever serve, so a single bypass on that host (an uploaded file, a JSONP-style endpoint, an open redirect serving script) unlocks execution for the whole policy, and broad allowlists are easy to misconfigure.
items.trap: The common intuition is that naming trusted CDNs is equivalent safety. Host allowlists are easier to bypass or misconfigure, which is why strict policies prefer nonce- or hash-based script-src tied to the exact scripts allowed for that response.

items.question: A review finds that the CSP nonce is generated once at deploy time and reused on every response for a week. Is that still a strict policy?
items.answer: No. The nonce must be unpredictable and match only the scripts intentionally emitted in that response. If it is static or predictable, any injection that can learn the nonce from a cached page, a log, or a previous response can simply carry it and execute. Generate a fresh high-entropy nonce per response and emit it only in the CSP header and the intended script tags.
items.trap: The naive view is 'the nonce is present, so the policy is strict'. A reused nonce degrades the mechanism into a shared secret that leaks with every response; unpredictability and per-response matching are the whole point.

items.question: The session cookie is HttpOnly, so XSS cannot steal it. Why does a stored XSS finding still get rated critical on this app?
items.answer: Because HttpOnly only blocks reading the cookie value through document.cookie. An injected script can still cause the browser to send authenticated requests while the cookie is attached: it can call your APIs, change the user's email or password, and act as the user without ever seeing the cookie value. That is why XSS must be fixed and sessions must be rotated and invalidated server-side.
items.trap: The common answer equates 'unreadable' with 'unusable'. Cookie attributes reduce theft and cross-site sending; they do not stop an XSS payload from causing requests while the browser attaches the cookie.

items.question: Why must a `__Host-` prefixed cookie omit `Domain` and use `Path=/`?
items.answer: The prefix is a promise the browser enforces: a cookie named `__Host-` must be Secure, set with `Path=/`, and without a `Domain` attribute. Omitting Domain pins the cookie to the exact host that set it, so a compromised or malicious subdomain cannot set or shadow a host-scoped session cookie. Allowing Domain would make the prefix guarantee meaningless.
items.trap: The naive answer treats the prefix as a naming convention. It is a browser-enforced contract: violating any of its rules makes the browser reject the cookie, and the rules exist specifically to prevent subdomain-scoped session cookies.

items.question: The team loves JWTs but needs instant revocation, so they add a Redis deny-list of revoked token IDs checked on every request. What did they actually build?
items.answer: A server-side session store with extra steps. Every request now hits a central lookup, which is exactly the cost opaque sessions pay, while the JWT-specific problems remain: key rotation, claim staleness, size, and audience validation. If revocation is a hard requirement, an opaque server session delivers the same guarantee more directly.
items.trap: The naive framing is 'we kept the stateless benefits and added revocation'. A per-request central lookup is not stateless; revocation is an explicit design problem for JWTs, and bolting a lookup on top rebuilds session semantics without session simplicity.

items.question: An admin demotes a compromised account, but the user's JWT says `role: admin` for another 23 hours. Why didn't the change take effect, and what are the honest options?
items.answer: Because JWT claims are a snapshot signed at issuance; a resource server validating without a central lookup has no way to know the claims are stale. The options are: short token lifetimes so staleness windows are small, reintroducing a lookup or introspection for sensitive claims, or moving authoritative state server-side with opaque sessions. Each trades away part of the stateless story.
items.trap: The common assumption is that signed means current. A signature proves who issued the token and that it was not tampered with, not that its claims still match reality; claim staleness is one of the explicit JWT trade-offs.

items.question: A frontend developer sends the OIDC ID Token to the API in the Authorization header, because 'it is signed and says who the user is'. What is wrong?
items.answer: Role confusion. The ID Token is the provider's signed statement about an authentication event, addressed to the client, for the client to establish who logged in. APIs must receive access tokens, whose audience is that resource server and whose scopes define what the call may do. Accepting ID Tokens at an API also breaks audience validation and revocation semantics.
items.trap: The naive answer is 'both are signed JWTs about the user, so either works'. The two token types have different audiences and purposes: access tokens for APIs, ID Tokens for the client; substituting one for the other is explicitly an anti-pattern.

items.question: The client requested the `openid` scope and received an ID Token. Before rendering 'Signed in as Alice', what must the client do with that token?
items.answer: Validate it according to the provider's published metadata and the OIDC rules: verify the signature with the provider's keys, check the issuer against the configured one, confirm the audience is this client, check expiration, and verify the nonce sent in the request matches the token's nonce claim. Only then may the client trust the identity claims.
items.trap: The common shortcut is decoding the payload and reading the claims because 'the provider sent it'. An ID Token is untrusted input until validated; the client validates it according to the provider's metadata and the protocol rules.

items.question: The token decodes cleanly and the payload shows the right issuer, audience, and a future exp. Why is the API still not allowed to accept it?
items.answer: Because decoding is not validation. Base64url decoding works on any bytes and proves nothing about who created the token. The API must verify the cryptographic signature using keys from the trusted authorization server, enforce an allowed algorithm (rejecting `alg=none`), and then evaluate issuer, audience, expiration, and required claims. A token that merely decodes is untrusted input.
items.trap: The naive answer conflates 'readable' with 'authentic'. The claims inside an unsigned or wrongly signed token can say anything, including the iss and aud you expect; only signature verification ties the claims to the issuer.

items.question: A gateway caches JWKS keys from five partner issuers in one pool and picks a key by trying them all. What can go wrong?
items.answer: Cross-issuer token confusion. A token issued by issuer A for audience A could be accepted by a resource expecting issuer B if the pool lets any cached key verify it and the issuer and audience checks are loose. Key selection must be constrained to the configured or discovered keys of the specific issuer being validated, with issuer and audience enforced per resource server.
items.trap: The naive answer is 'if some trusted key verifies the signature, the token is fine'. Signature validity only means 'signed by that key's owner'; whether that owner is the issuer this API trusts, and whether the token was issued for this audience, are separate mandatory checks.

items.question: If PKCE already protects the flow, why is a `state` value still required alongside it?
items.answer: They defend against different attacks. PKCE ensures that whoever redeems the authorization code at the token endpoint must know the verifier, blocking code interception. state binds the response to the initiating browser session: without it, an attacker can forge or substitute an authorization response (request forgery) or mix up responses from multiple providers, logging the victim into the wrong session. PKCE says nothing about whether the response belongs to this request.
items.trap: The common answer treats PKCE as a total defense for the OAuth flow. It protects the code exchange only; request forgery and response mix-up are exactly what a session-bound state value plus an exact registered redirect URI prevent.

items.question: The SPA keeps its access token in localStorage because cookies 'have too many rules'. What is the security trade-off?
items.answer: Anything that achieves script execution on the page (an XSS or a malicious dependency) can read localStorage and exfiltrate the token, extending the compromise beyond the browser session. The preferred alternatives: keep tokens out of the browser with a backend-for-frontend that holds them server-side and issues an HttpOnly cookie session, and always keep tokens out of URLs and logs.
items.trap: The naive comparison is cookie attributes versus storage convenience. The real question is exposure to script: localStorage is fully readable by any script on the page, so a token there turns every XSS into token theft; a BFF or HttpOnly cookie session removes that read access.

items.question: An engineer committed a live cloud provider key to a private branch. They delete the file and force-push a clean history. Is the incident over?
items.answer: No. The value already left the trust boundary: refs, clones, CI logs, and anyone who fetched the branch still have it, and history rewriting revokes nothing. The correct response is to treat the credential as exposed: rotate or revoke it immediately, audit what it accessed, then clean up. Repository scanning is detection; rotation and revocation are the control.
items.trap: The naive answer assumes 'not in the current commit' equals 'not known'. A committed secret must be considered exposed the moment it landed in git; deleting the file only hides the evidence.

items.question: One database password is shared by the staging and production deployments of three services 'to keep config simple'. Why does the secrets guidance call this out?
items.answer: Because sharing expands blast radius and weakens accountability: one leak in the least protected context (a staging box, a debug log) exposes production, and audit trails cannot attribute reads to a specific workload. The guidance is to separate environments and grant each workload only the specific values it needs, so a single exposure is contained and traceable.
items.trap: The naive answer optimizes for operational simplicity and treats a secret as a config value. Secrets are per-context capabilities; least privilege per workload and environment is the rule, and sharing is what turns a small leak into a broad incident.

items.question: Login is rate-limited strictly by source IP. Name the two ways this design fails in opposite directions.
items.answer: First, evasion: credential-stuffing botnets rotate IPs, so a distributed attack stays under each address's threshold while a per-IP limit barely slows it. Second, collateral damage: legitimate users behind shared NAT (a campus, an office, a mobile carrier) get locked out because thousands of people share one address. The fix is to key limits on the account or tenant as well, enforce them at a trusted shared edge, and combine throttling with monitoring and account-risk controls.
items.trap: The naive answer picks IP because it is the identifier that is always available. A single IP-only limit is easy to evade and can punish shared networks, which is exactly the failure pair the design guidance warns about.

items.question: The login limiter returns 429 with a body: 'Too many attempts for user@example.com, try later'. What did the implementation leak?
items.answer: Whether that account exists. An attacker probing usernames gets a different signal for real accounts than for random addresses, enabling enumeration ahead of phishing or targeting. The guidance is to avoid revealing whether an account exists: return a generic 429 with a safe retry hint such as Retry-After, and keep responses uniform across valid and invalid identifiers.
items.trap: The naive review only checks that the limiter returns 429 and a retry hint. The content of the response matters: anything that distinguishes existing accounts from nonexistent ones turns a protective control into an enumeration oracle.

items.question: The site is HTTPS-only. A reviewer still flags session fixation on the login form. How is that possible if the transport is encrypted?
items.answer: Because fixation is not about reading traffic; it is about causing the victim to authenticate with an identifier the attacker already knows. The attacker can plant a known identifier in the victim's browser through another channel, and if the application keeps using that identifier after login, the attacker reuses it. TLS protects the wire, not the provenance of the identifier: the fix is to regenerate the session identifier at authentication and treat any client-supplied identifier as untrusted input.
items.trap: The naive answer maps every session attack to eavesdropping and assumes encryption closes the class. TLS alone does not prevent fixation; rotation after authentication is the control.

items.question: The team rotates the session ID at login. Their admin panel promotes a user to administrator without touching the session. What did they miss?
items.answer: Privilege changes are the second mandatory rotation point. An identifier issued under an anonymous or standard role should not survive elevation to a higher-privilege role: regenerate after any privilege change, invalidate the old identifier, preserve only server-side state that is safe to carry over, and deliver the new value with secure cookie attributes.
items.trap: The naive answer treats login as the only fixation moment. The attack class is 'identifier issued under lower trust, reused under higher trust', which is exactly what happens at role elevation; that is why rotation is required after authentication and after privilege changes.

items.question: The API gateway checks the Origin against `*.partner.acme.test` and echoes the request Origin back in Access-Control-Allow-Origin when it matches. Why is this flagged in review?
items.answer: Two issues. First, the response must be one exact origin from a controlled, tenant-aware allowlist, never an arbitrary reflection; echoing whatever matched a pattern admits any origin satisfying it, including hosts a tenant stood up without review. Second, wildcard subdomain trust is not tenant-aware: any host under that suffix, including a compromised or attacker-registered subdomain, becomes a credentialed reader of the API.
items.trap: The naive answer is 'we validate against a pattern, so it is controlled'. Pattern reflection is not an allowlist: the review standard is an explicit inventory of browser clients, one exact allowed origin returned, and tenant authorization enforced independently of CORS.

items.question: Responses include Access-Control-Allow-Origin only for allowlisted origins, but the CDN in front of the API caches them without any Origin awareness. What breaks?
items.answer: Cache poisoning of the CORS headers. The CDN can cache a response negotiated for one origin (with that origin's ACAO and credentials flag) and serve it to a different origin's request, either breaking legitimate clients or handing a disallowed origin a cached response that appears to permit its read. Any response that varies by Origin must carry `Vary: Origin` so intermediaries key their cache on it.
items.trap: The naive answer stops at 'the server computes the right headers per request'. CORS correctness is per request-response pair; without `Vary: Origin`, an intermediary can silently re-pair a cached response with the wrong origin, which is why the guidance requires it when responses differ by Origin.

items.question: The repo pins every dependency with a lockfile and CI installs with a frozen lockfile. Why does the supply-chain review still find gaps?
items.answer: Pinning prevents drift, not compromise. The pinned versions can still get a new advisory tomorrow; install scripts still execute untrusted package code in CI where secrets live; a private scope that is not protected can be resolved from a public registry (dependency confusion); and artifacts can be tampered with if nothing verifies checksums or signatures. The control set is lockfiles plus a controlled proxy or internal registry, integrity verification, install-script review, isolated builds, and continuous monitoring of vulnerability sources.
items.trap: The naive answer equates reproducible installs with secure installs. A lockfile is a consistency control; vulnerable pinned versions, malicious install scripts, dependency confusion, and tampered artifacts each need their own controls.

items.question: Your package `@acme/ui` exists only in your internal registry. Where does dependency confusion come from, and what stops it?
items.answer: It comes from resolvers that fall back to public registries: if a build or a developer machine resolves `@acme/ui` from a public registry, an attacker who published that exact name there feeds you their code. The defenses are to protect the private package scope (registry-side reservation and access control), route package retrieval through a controlled proxy or internal registry that does not silently fall back, and verify checksums or signatures so substituted artifacts fail.
items.trap: The naive answer is 'nobody outside knows the name, so it cannot be taken'. Public registries do not check your internal naming; if any resolution path can reach them, an unclaimed name is claimable by anyone, which is why protecting private scopes against dependency confusion is an explicit control.

items.question: A scanner files a ticket: CVSS 9.8 in a transitive dependency your service pulls in. The vulnerable code path is a parser your service never invokes. Do you page the on-call and deploy tonight?
items.answer: No, you investigate first. Identify the affected version and dependency path, confirm the advisory with a trusted vulnerability source, and determine whether the deployed product is reachable and exploitable: an unreachable code path with compensating controls is a different risk than an exposed one. Patching follows exploitability and exposure, not the scanner's severity number; the finding still gets an owner, a deadline, and a documented decision.
items.trap: The naive answer treats the CVSS score as the priority. Severity measures the vulnerability's worst case, not your exposure; blindly applying a score wastes emergency change windows on unreachable code, and in the inverse case under-prioritizes a lower-scored, directly exploitable path.

items.question: The advisory affects version 2.x, your app pins 2.3.1, and no fixed release exists yet. What are your options besides waiting?
items.answer: Work the alternatives in order of preference: upgrade the direct dependency if any version pulls a fixed transitive one; apply a vendor patch if one ships outside the mainline; replace the component; or add a narrowly scoped mitigation (blocking the vulnerable entry point, a WAF rule, disabling the affected feature) while tracking an owner and a deadline. If risk is accepted, document it with an accountable approver and keep monitoring until the component is patched or removed.
items.trap: The naive answer is a binary 'upgrade or wait'. When no fixed version exists, the playbook is containment plus accountability: mitigation, replacement, or formally accepted risk with an owner, because waiting without a tracked decision is how vulnerable components survive for years.

items.question: A CI token leaks into a public build log. The platform team deletes the log within an hour. Why does the incident response guidance say that is not containment?
items.answer: Because deletion does not revoke. Anyone or any scraper that captured the log in that window holds a live credential, and copies persist in caches, mirrors, and archives. The required action is to revoke the exposed value and issue a replacement, then audit what it accessed. Detection (finding secrets in logs, repos, artifacts, and images) is the trigger; revocation is the control.
items.trap: The naive answer confuses removing the copy with removing the capability. A secret is a capability held by whoever saw it; you must revoke exposed values, not merely delete the file or log where they appeared.

items.question: You are asked to secure the secret manager itself. Its unseal and bootstrap credentials are long-lived and shared by the on-call team. Why is that a first-class finding, not an internal detail?
items.answer: Because those credentials are the root of the trust tree: whoever holds them can read or rewrap everything the organization stores, and a shared, long-lived value has no attribution and no natural expiry. The guidance is to model the secret manager's own bootstrap credentials and recovery path as sensitive assets: issue separate, short-lived or workload-bound credentials, log administrative changes centrally, and design emergency rotation and recovery before an incident, including how to reach the secret system if it is down.
items.trap: The naive answer focuses only on application secrets and treats the manager's own access as infrastructure plumbing. The bootstrap path is the highest-blast-radius credential in the system; leaving it shared and long-lived recreates exactly the blast-radius problem the program exists to remove.

mcqs.question: According to the OWASP XSS Prevention Cheat Sheet, what is the primary defense against XSS?
options: Contextual output encoding of untrusted values at the point where they are rendered
A strict Content-Security-Policy header on every response
Blacklisting dangerous characters like < and > on input
Serving the application exclusively over HTTPS
mcqs.explanation: OWASP positions context-aware output encoding (HTML, attribute, URL, or JavaScript context) as the primary XSS defense, with sanitization reserved for cases where users must author HTML. The strongest distractor is the CSP option: CSP is a useful additional layer, but OWASP does not recommend it as the primary XSS defense. Blacklisting is explicitly rejected in favor of encoding, and HTTPS protects transport, not script injection.

mcqs.question: A user-supplied value is rendered as an href attribute. The template HTML-encodes it, but an attacker submits `javascript:alert(1)` and it executes on click. What went wrong?
options: Nothing; HTML encoding makes the value inert in every position
The value was encoded for the wrong context: an href is a URL context and needs URL handling plus a scheme allowlist
The app should have stripped the quotes around the attribute
The anchor tag needed a CSP nonce
mcqs.explanation: Encoding must match the output context. In an href the browser interprets the value as a URL, and `javascript:` is valid URL syntax, so HTML entity encoding does not neutralize it; the fix is URL-context handling with an allowed scheme (http or https) or relative paths. The first option is the trap: HTML encoding protects markup structure, not URL semantics. Stripping quotes does not affect the scheme, and CSP is a mitigating layer that does not fix the injection point.

mcqs.question: A team sets SameSite=Lax on the session cookie and proposes deleting all CSRF token logic. What is the strongest objection?
options: SameSite is only supported by experimental browsers
SameSite is defense in depth: Lax still sends the cookie on top-level GET navigations, so state-changing endpoints still need server-validated tokens and must stay out of GET
SameSite=Lax blocks all cross-site image loads and breaks analytics
CSRF tokens are mandated by the HTTP specification
mcqs.explanation: The guidance is that every state-changing endpoint needs a server-validated CSRF token, with SameSite and Origin or Fetch Metadata checks as defense in depth; Lax cookies still travel on top-level cross-site GET navigations, which is also why state changes must never be reachable via GET. The strongest distractor claims broad SameSite support is missing, which is false for current browsers. The image-load claim misdescribes the mechanism (it governs cookie attachment, not loading), and no HTTP spec mandates tokens.

mcqs.question: What does CORS actually control?
options: Which origins a browser will let script read responses from
Which origins are allowed to send requests to the server
Which users are authenticated for cross-origin calls
The TLS requirements for cross-origin traffic
mcqs.explanation: CORS is an HTTP-header mechanism by which a server declares which other origins a browser may read through APIs such as fetch; the same-origin policy plus CORS govern browser read access. The second option is the classic inversion: cross-origin requests (form posts, images, non-preflighted calls) are still sent, and CORS decides whether the response can be read. CORS is not an authentication mechanism and says nothing about TLS.

mcqs.question: A credentialed fetch (credentials: 'include') is answered with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` and `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. What does the browser do?
options: Allows the response because both headers are present
Blocks the response: a wildcard allowed origin cannot be combined with credentialed requests
Downgrades the request to non-credentialed and retries
Sends an extra preflight to confirm with the server
mcqs.explanation: For credentialed requests the server must name one explicit allowed origin and allow credentials; `*` cannot be combined with credentials, so the browser refuses to expose the response. The first option is exactly the misconfiguration the rule exists to catch. There is no downgrade-and-retry behavior, and the constraint concerns response readability, not an additional preflight.

mcqs.question: What does the HttpOnly cookie attribute actually prevent?
options: Cross-site requests from attaching the cookie
The cookie being sent over plain HTTP
Page scripts reading the cookie through document.cookie
A subdomain from receiving the cookie
mcqs.explanation: HttpOnly makes the cookie inaccessible to page script via document.cookie, removing one exfiltration path for the session identifier. Cross-site sending is governed by SameSite, HTTPS-only transport by Secure, and host scoping by Domain and Path or the `__Host-` prefix. Note the limit, which the other options miss: HttpOnly does not stop an XSS payload from causing authenticated requests while the browser attaches the cookie.

mcqs.question: A product needs instant logout, admin-driven revocation, and permission changes that take effect immediately. Which representation fits most naturally, and why?
options: JWTs, because they are signed and cannot be forged
Opaque server-side sessions, because authoritative state stays server-side, making revocation, logout, and permission changes straightforward
JWTs with very long expiry, because fewer token requests means fewer revocation problems
Either one, because revocation difficulty is a myth
mcqs.explanation: With an opaque session the server holds the authoritative state and the browser only carries a random identifier, so logout, revocation, and permission changes are direct operations on that state. The strongest distractor confuses integrity with revocability: a valid signature does not help you invalidate a token before expiry, which is exactly the JWT trade-off. Long expiry makes claim staleness worse, and the last option denies a well-documented design problem.

mcqs.question: In an OpenID Connect login, what is the ID Token for?
options: Calling the user's APIs on their behalf
Letting the client learn and confirm who authenticated, after validating the token
Refreshing the access token when it expires
Proving to the browser that the provider's TLS certificate is valid
mcqs.explanation: OIDC adds an identity layer on OAuth 2.0: the client requests the `openid` scope and receives a signed ID Token containing claims about the authentication event and the user, which the client validates against the provider's metadata before trusting it. The strongest distractor is the first: access tokens are for calling protected resources, while the ID Token's audience is the client, not an API. Refresh tokens handle renewal, and TLS is unrelated to OIDC.

mcqs.question: An API receives a JWT access token. Which set of checks must pass before the request is authorized?
options: The payload decodes and exp is in the future
The token is signed with any key in the verifier's cache and has a sub claim
Signature verification with the issuer's keys, an enforced allowed algorithm, and issuer, audience, and expiration validation for this resource server
The token was received over HTTPS and is under 4 KB
mcqs.explanation: A JWT is untrusted input until validation succeeds: verify the signature with keys from the trusted authorization server, enforce an allowed algorithm (rejecting `alg=none`), and validate issuer, audience, expiration, and required claims; the JWT profile for OAuth access tokens specifically requires audience and signature validation. The strongest distractor is the first: decoding is not validation, since anyone can craft an unsigned token with any claims. Key possession without issuer trust allows cross-issuer confusion, and transport hygiene is not token validation.

mcqs.question: In the authorization code flow with PKCE for a browser SPA, what does the PKCE verifier specifically prevent?
options: An intercepted authorization code from being redeemed, because the token endpoint requires the verifier that matches the challenge
The client secret from leaking in browser code
An attacker from forging or substituting the authorization response in the victim's browser
The access token from appearing in server logs
mcqs.explanation: PKCE binds code redemption to the party that started the flow: the client sends a challenge derived from a high-entropy verifier, and the token endpoint only redeems the code when presented with the matching verifier, so a stolen code is useless. The strongest distractor misunderstands the threat: public browser clients have no secret to protect, which is why PKCE exists. Forged or substituted responses are what the session-bound state value prevents, and keeping tokens out of logs is an operational practice.

mcqs.question: A live credential is discovered in a public repository's history. What is the correct first response?
options: Delete the file, force-push the branch, and close the finding
Add the path to .gitignore so future commits are clean
Revoke or rotate the credential immediately, then audit its usage, treating every copy in history as compromised
Rename the variable and obfuscate the value in the next release
mcqs.explanation: A committed secret must be treated as exposed the moment it landed in git: clones, forks, and archives retain it, so the control is revocation or rotation, followed by auditing what the credential accessed. The strongest distractor is the force-push: history rewriting hides evidence but revokes nothing. Adding the path to .gitignore prevents future commits of that path but does nothing about the leaked value, and obfuscation is not secrecy.

mcqs.question: Your organization uses an internal registry for `@corp/*` packages, but a developer's laptop falls back to the public npm registry when the VPN is down. Which supply-chain risk does this create, and what is the control?
options: Typosquatting: users mistype package names; the control is code review

Dependency confusion: an attacker publishes `@corp/...` names publicly and your build resolves their code; the control is protecting private scopes and routing retrieval through a controlled proxy or internal registry without silent fallback
Lockfile drift: versions change between builds; the control is a frozen lockfile
License violations: packages ship under incompatible licenses; the control is an SBOM
mcqs.explanation: Dependency confusion happens when a resolver can reach a public registry for a name that should only exist privately: an attacker registers the unclaimed public name and your build executes their install code. The controls are protecting private package scopes and routing package retrieval through a controlled proxy or internal registry. The strongest distractor is the lockfile: it is a consistency control, and if a public resolution ever lands in it, the attacker's version is pinned and locked in. Typosquatting and license risk are real but different problems.

scenarios.prompt: Review this Express route for security defects. Identify every issue, explain the impact, and describe the fix for each.
scenarios.modelAnswer: There are two defects. (1) Reflected XSS: `name` from the query string is concatenated into the HTML body with no encoding, so a payload like an img tag with an onerror handler executes in the victim's browser. The primary defense is contextual output encoding: escape the value for the HTML context before interpolation, or use a template engine that escapes by default and treat raw-HTML escape hatches as security-sensitive. (2) The CSP nonce is static: it is generated once at deploy time and reused on every response, so it is predictable and shared. Anyone who can observe one response (a cached page, a log, a referring page) learns the nonce, and an injected script can carry it and execute, defeating the policy. The nonce must be a fresh, unpredictable value per response, emitted only in that response's CSP header and its intended script tags. Layering matters: even a correct nonce policy is a second layer that reduces XSS impact; it does not replace encoding or sanitization (OWASP XSS Prevention Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Cross_Site_Scripting_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html; MDN CSP guide: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CSP). Fixed shape: generate the nonce per request with a crypto-random value, HTML-encode `name`, keep `default-src 'self'`, and add only the directives the page actually needs.
rubric: Identifies the unencoded interpolation of req.query.name into HTML as reflected XSS and names contextual output encoding as the primary fix
Explains why a static, deploy-time nonce defeats nonce-based CSP: the nonce must be unpredictable and unique per response
Recognizes that CSP is a mitigating layer and does not replace encoding or sanitization
Proposes a correct fix: per-response crypto-random nonce plus HTML-escaped output
Does not attempt to fix it with input blacklisting or by trusting the CSP alone

scenarios.prompt: You are reviewing a credentialed CORS design for a multi-tenant API. This middleware runs in front of every route. Find the defects and redesign it.
scenarios.modelAnswer: The middleware reflects the request Origin instead of consulting the tenant allowlist it defines, and it pairs that reflection with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. Reflection plus credentials means any origin on the internet, including an attacker-controlled page, is told it may read credentialed responses from this API: the browser attaches the victim's cookies and then lets the attacker's script read the response. That is a cross-origin data exposure, not a cosmetic misconfiguration. Additional defects: (1) No Vary: Origin, so a CDN or proxy can cache a response negotiated for one origin and serve it to another. (2) Access-Control-Allow-Headers reflects the preflight's requested headers verbatim, which validates nothing. (3) The tenant map is dead code: the design standard is to compare the request Origin against a controlled, tenant-aware allowlist and return one exact allowed origin, never an arbitrary reflection. (4) Most importantly, CORS is a browser read policy, not authorization: even a correct CORS layer does not excuse the API from enforcing tenant authorization on every request, and cookie SameSite policy and CSRF defenses must be reviewed together with this change. Fixed design: look up the tenant's allowlist, set ACAO to that exact origin on a match, add Vary: Origin whenever the response depends on it, allow credentials only where a tenant genuinely needs them, and validate preflight methods and headers against a fixed list (MDN CORS configuration guidance: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Security/Practical_implementation_guides/CORS).
rubric: Flags arbitrary Origin reflection combined with Allow-Credentials as a credentialed cross-origin read exposure
Requires an exact, tenant-aware allowlist match that returns one specific origin
Adds Vary: Origin for responses that differ by Origin, and explains the caching hazard without it
Treats CORS as a browser read policy, not authorization, and keeps tenant authorization server-side
Connects the change to cookie SameSite and CSRF posture instead of reviewing CORS in isolation

scenarios.prompt: This authentication middleware guards every API route. Find every validation flaw and describe the correct order of operations.
scenarios.modelAnswer: The middleware fails before it even verifies: it decodes the token and trusts the unverified iss claim to select the verification key, so an attacker chooses which key gets tried by editing the header of an unsigned token. The algorithm list accepts 'none', which means a token with alg=none and no signature can pass verification outright, and mixing HS256 with RS256 invites algorithm confusion, where an attacker signs using the RSA public key treated as an HMAC secret. There is no audience check, so a token issued for a different resource server (or an ID Token, whose audience is a client) would be accepted here, and there is no issuer allowlist: any issuer present in the shared cache is trusted. The manual exp check is redundant and incomplete: nothing validates iss or aud for this API. Correct order of operations, per the JWT profile for OAuth access tokens (RFC 9068: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9068.html): determine the expected issuer first, fetch keys only from that issuer's configured or discovered JWKS, verify the signature with a single enforced algorithm family while rejecting alg=none, then validate iss, aud (this resource server), exp, and required scopes, and build req.user from the verified claims only. Also distinguish access tokens from ID Tokens: an ID Token must never be accepted as an API credential.
rubric: Identifies decode-before-verify as trusting unverified claims for key selection
Flags the acceptance of alg=none and the HS256/RS256 mix as signature-bypass and algorithm-confusion risks
Requires audience and issuer validation for this resource server, citing the access-token profile requirement
Constrains key selection to the specific issuer's keys rather than a shared multi-issuer cache
Builds authorization state from verified claims and keeps endpoint scope policy enforcement separate

scenarios.prompt: A penetration test reports that an attacker can log in as a victim whose session identifier was planted beforehand. Review this login and promotion flow, explain the vulnerability, and fix it.
scenarios.modelAnswer: The reported vulnerability is session fixation: the handler accepts a session identifier supplied by the client (req.cookies['session']) and keeps using it after authentication. An attacker who can plant a known identifier in the victim's browser (a crafted link, a cookie set by a vulnerable subdomain) waits for the victim to log in and then reuses that identifier, because the server never regenerates it. The fix is to always generate a fresh session identifier at authentication, invalidate any old identifier, and deliver the new one with Secure, HttpOnly, and the narrowest viable SameSite. Second defect: SameSite=None is chosen although nothing in this flow needs cross-site sending; Lax (or Strict, if the product permits) reduces cross-site exposure and complements the CSRF posture. Third: /promote elevates the session to admin without rotating the identifier; rotation is required after authentication and after privilege changes, preserving only server-side state that is safe to carry over. Adjacent gaps worth naming: no visible rate limiting or credential-stuffing protection on /login, and no idle or absolute expiration. The uniform 'invalid email or password' message is the one thing done right, since it avoids revealing whether the account exists (OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Session_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html).
rubric: Identifies session fixation: the client-supplied sid survives authentication instead of being regenerated
Requires rotation after privilege changes, not only at login, plus invalidation of the old identifier
Questions SameSite=None, preferring Lax or Strict unless a documented cross-site need exists
Adds server-side session hygiene: expiration, invalidation at logout, and login rate limiting
Recognizes that TLS and Secure cookies do not prevent fixation, since the attack concerns identifier provenance
